body_html:
A mobile SEO checklist makes sure the mobile version of your site, which Google uses to crawl and index it, has the same content, links, and metadata as desktop, loads quickly on a phone, and is easy to use with a thumb. Here's what to check and how to fix common problems.

Why the mobile version is the one that counts

Google finished its move to mobile-first indexing in October 2023. In plain terms, Google crawls your site with a smartphone bot and builds its index from what that bot sees. If something exists on desktop but not on mobile, Google may not see it at all.

The testing tools changed too. Google retired the Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report in Search Console in December 2023, as announced on the Search Central blog, and pointed people to Lighthouse instead. Many older checklists still tell you to run the retired tool, so here's what to use now.

You want to checkUse now
Speed and usability on a phoneLighthouse in Chrome DevTools (mobile mode) or PageSpeed Insights
What Google's smartphone bot actually rendersURL Inspection live test in Search Console (screenshot and rendered HTML)
Real-user speed by deviceCore Web Vitals report in Search Console (mobile and desktop shown separately)
Content parity across the whole siteTwo crawls, one with a smartphone user agent and one with desktop

Which mobile setup do you have?

How much of this checklist applies depends on how your site serves phones. Google's mobile site and mobile-first indexing best practices describe three setups.

Responsive

  • One URL and the same HTML for every screen
  • Content and metadata match by default
  • Google recommends it as easiest to maintain
  • Focus on layout, speed, and pop-ups

Dynamic serving

  • One URL, different HTML per device
  • Should send the Vary: user-agent header
  • Parity can drift: compare both versions
  • Check robots meta tags on the mobile HTML

Separate URLs (m-dot)

  • A different address, often m.yoursite.com
  • Needs canonical and alternate tags
  • Verify both versions in Search Console
  • Most places for mistakes

My decision rule: if your site is responsive, the parity items below rarely fail, so spend most of your time on speed and pop-ups. If it uses dynamic serving or m-dot URLs, start with parity, because that's where pages quietly drop out of the index.

The mobile SEO checklist

Tick items off as you go; your progress is saved in this browser.

Content and links

  • Main text and headings match desktop (tabs and accordions are fine if the content is in the page)
  • Primary content doesn't load only after a tap, swipe, or typing, since Google's bot won't take those actions
  • Mobile menus still link to important category and service pages
  • Images use the same URLs and alt text as desktop, and aren't too small or low resolution

Metadata and structured data

  • Title tags and meta descriptions match desktop
  • Robots meta tags match desktop, with no mobile-only noindex or nofollow
  • The same structured data appears on mobile pages, with mobile URLs inside it on m-dot sites
  • robots.txt doesn't block CSS, JavaScript, or images the mobile pages need

Layout and usability

  • A viewport meta tag is set to the device width
  • Nothing scrolls sideways, and text is readable without pinching to zoom
  • Buttons and links are big enough, and far enough apart, to tap accurately
  • No full-screen pop-up covers the content right after someone lands

Watch out A noindex or nofollow that appears only on mobile can drop pages from search, because the mobile version is the one Google indexes. This often comes from a plugin or theme setting that serves different code to phones. Check the robots meta tag in the URL Inspection rendered HTML, not just in your desktop browser.

Speed on a phone

Core Web Vitals are Google's measures of loading (LCP), responsiveness (INP), and visual stability (CLS). Here are the "good" marks:

2.5 sLCP "good" limit (web.dev)

200 msINP "good" limit (web.dev)

0.1CLS "good" limit (web.dev)

Mobile is usually the weaker of the two in the Core Web Vitals report. Oversized images, heavy sliders, and stacks of third-party scripts are the usual culprits. My page speed optimization work starts there.

On pop-ups, Google's guidance on intrusive interstitials and dialogs calls out full-screen dialogs that cover the content, such as newsletter or app-install prompts. Small banners that take up a fraction of the screen are fine, and legally required ones, such as an age gate, are treated differently.

How to find mobile SEO issues on your site

  1. Run a URL Inspection live test

    Test your homepage and one page per template. If the screenshot looks broken or blank, check for blocked CSS or JavaScript first.

  2. Run Lighthouse in mobile mode

    Use Chrome DevTools or PageSpeed Insights on the same URLs for speed and usability checks.

  3. Compare two crawls

    Crawl once with a smartphone user agent and once with desktop, then compare word counts, titles, links, and structured data. Big gaps point to parity problems.

  4. Use your own phone

    Tap through your top pages and forms on cellular data, not office wifi. Many problems are obvious in thirty seconds.

Is mobile-first indexing the same as being mobile-friendly?

No. Mobile-first indexing is about which version of your site Google reads: the mobile one. Mobile-friendliness is about whether people can comfortably use that version. A site can be indexed mobile-first and still frustrate visitors with tiny text or pop-ups. A good mobile SEO checklist covers both: content parity for indexing, and layout, speed, and usability for the people who land on the page.

Does Google still have a mobile-friendly test?

Not as a standalone tool. Google retired the Mobile-Friendly Test and the Mobile Usability report in December 2023. For the same kinds of checks, use Lighthouse in Chrome or PageSpeed Insights for speed and usability, and the URL Inspection tool in Search Console to see the mobile page Google renders. Core Web Vitals data by device is still in Search Console.

Do you need responsive design for mobile SEO?

It isn't required, but Google recommends it. Responsive design uses one URL and one set of HTML for every screen size, so there's no risk of the mobile version falling out of sync with desktop. Separate mobile sites can still rank, but they need careful canonical tags, matching content, and matching robots rules, which adds ongoing work and more places for mistakes.
